## Data
```{r, message = FALSE}
lapd <- read_csv("Police_Payroll.csv")
```

Let's clean names and subset data to only focus on the year 2018, and the variables `job_class_title`, `employment_type`, and `base_pay`. Then reassign it to `lapd`.

--

```{r}
lapd <- clean_names(lapd) |> 
  filter(year == 2018) |> 
  select(job_class_title, 
         employment_type, 
         base_pay)
```

---

```{r}
glimpse(lapd)
```

---

## Creating New Variables

To create a new variable we use the function `mutate()`, with the data set as the first argument, then specifications on how we want to create the new variable in subsequent arguments. Or we can pipe the data set to the function. 

New variables will be added to the right of the other variables. 

---

### Creating new variables using operations between existing variables

We can use an existing numerical variable in a mathematical expression to define the new numerical variable. 
 
---

### Example 1

Create a new variable called `base_pay_k` that represents `base_pay` in thousand of dollars.

--

Note that we first define the new variable before the equal sign within the mutate() function.

```{r}
lapd |> 
  mutate(base_pay_k = base_pay/1000)
```

---

### Creating new variables based on conditions

**Two conditions**

When we have **two outcomes** of a condition, either or, then we can utilize the `if_else()` function to define our conditions.


```{r echo = FALSE, out.width="40%"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/if-else.PNG")
```

---

### Example 2

According to Business Insider, in 2018, a household was considered "wealthy" or upper class if they earn more than $188,000 annually.

Let's say we wanted to classify LAPD staff as wealthy or not. 

---

we can create a variable called "wealth_status". If the base_pay is “more than 188000” for any row then the wealth_status" will be set to “wealthy”, else (i.e., if the base_pay is “less than or equal to 188000”) wealth_status will be set to “not wealthy”.

```{r}
mutate(lapd, wealth_status = if_else(base_pay > 188000,
      "wealthy",
      "not wealthy"))
```


---

**More than two conditions**

Sometimes we need to create variables based on **multiple conditions** rather than just two. The `case_when()` function is perfect for these situations where we have more than two possible conditions and actions.

In such case, we create a new categorical variable, where its categories correspond to intervals created from braking the range of a numerical variable. 

We use the function `case_when()` inside `mutate()`.

---

### Example 3

Create a new variable called `base_pay_level` which has `Less Than 0`, `No Income`, `Greater than 0 and less than Median` and `Greater than Median`. We will consider $62474 as the median (from previous lecture).

--

Let's first check if there is anyone earning exactly the median value.

```{r}
lapd |> 
  filter(base_pay == 62474)
```

There is no one earning the median, hence we can use the strictly "less than" or "greater than" operators to create our conditions. 

---

```{r}
lapd |> 
  mutate(base_pay_level = case_when(
    base_pay < 0 ~ "Less than 0", 
    base_pay == 0 ~ "No Income",
    base_pay > 0 & base_pay < 62474 ~ "Greater than 0 and less than Median",
    base_pay > 62474 ~ "Greater than Median")) 
```

---

We can't really __see__ what we have created. 

```{r}
lapd |> 
  mutate(base_pay_level = case_when(
    base_pay < 0 ~ "Less than 0", 
    base_pay == 0 ~ "No Income",
    base_pay < 62474 & base_pay > 0 ~ "Less than Median, Greater than 0",
    base_pay > 62474 ~ "Greater than Median")) |> 
  select(base_pay_level)
```


---

We can visualize the new variable we have created.

.left-panel[
```{r eval = FALSE}
lapd |> 
  mutate(base_pay_level = case_when(
    base_pay < 0 ~ "Less than 0", 
    base_pay == 0 ~ "No Income",
    base_pay < 62474 & base_pay > 0 ~ "Less than Median, Greater than 0",
    base_pay > 62474 ~ "Greater than Median")) |> 
  select(base_pay_level) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = base_pay_level)) +
  geom_bar()
```

We can use pipes with ggplot too!
]

.right-panel[
```{r echo = FALSE}
lapd |> 
  mutate(base_pay_level = case_when(
    base_pay < 0 ~ "Less than 0", 
    base_pay == 0 ~ "No Income",
    base_pay < 62474 & base_pay > 0 ~ "Less than Median, Greater than 0",
    base_pay > 62474 ~ "Greater than Median")) |> 
  select(base_pay_level) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = base_pay_level)) +
  geom_bar()
```
]

---

```{r}
glimpse(lapd)
```

__Note__: the data remains unchanged unless we "save" it. You may choose to save as you go; however, as we work on data cleaning and creating variables, it makes sense not to "save" the data frames. Once we see the final data frame we want then we can "save" (i.e. overwrite) it.

---

## Changing a variable type

There will be times when R does not assign the correct variable type or when you want to change it based on the analysis you want to do on it. 

We use one of the following functions inside `mutate()` to assign the correct variable type. 

`as.factor()` - makes a vector factor  
`as.numeric()` - makes a vector numeric  
`as.integer()` - makes a vector integer  
`as.double()` - makes a vector double  
`as.character()` - makes a vector character

---

### Example 4

```{r}
glimpse(lapd)
```


Change `job_class_title` and `employment_type` to factor variables. 


---

```{r}
lapd |> 
  mutate(employment_type = as.factor(employment_type),
         job_class_title = as.factor(job_class_title)) 
```

---

class: middle

Now that we know the final data frame that we want, we can now "save" (i.e. overwrite) it.


```{r}
lapd <- lapd |> 
    mutate(employment_type = as.factor(employment_type),
           job_class_title = as.factor(job_class_title),
           base_pay_k = base_pay/1000,
           wealth_status = if_else(base_pay > 188000,
                                   "wealthy",
                                   "not wealthy"),
           base_pay_level = case_when(
             base_pay < 0 ~ "Less than 0", 
             base_pay == 0 ~ "No Income",
             base_pay < 62474 & base_pay > 0 ~ "Less than Median, Greater than 0",
             base_pay > 62474 ~ "Greater than Median"))
```

---

Take a look at the data set to verify that the changes were made and saved.

```{r}
glimpse(lapd)
```

---

class: middle

### Word of caution

The functions `clean_names()`, `select()`, `filter()`, `slice()`, and `mutate()` take a data frame as the first argument. When we use `|>`, the data frame is piped through from the previous step of code at each step. When we use these functions without the `|>` we have to include the data frame explicitly.

.pull-left[
Data frame is used as the first argument
```{r}
select(lapd, base_pay)
```
]

.pull-right[
Data frame is piped

```{r}
lapd |> 
  select(base_pay)
```
]
